read: full: abstract, sections 1-5, appendix A.6 (human evaluation) and B (checklist); the AMPS module lists (pp. 18-22) and references skimmed
venue_now: NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p1 footer); arXiv 2103.03874v2, 8 Nov 2021. The May entry cites the arXiv preprint.
what_it_is: MATH is a set of 12,500 competition mathematics problems (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME and others, collected via AoPS; the problems were created by the MAA) in seven subjects with difficulty levels 1 to 5, split 7,500 train / 5,000 test; every problem has a full step-by-step LaTeX solution ending in a boxed answer (p1, p4, p17). Models are scored by exact match of the normalised boxed answer (p5). The paper also releases AMPS, a pretraining corpus of over 100K Khan Academy problems and about 5M problems generated by 100 hand-designed Mathematica scripts (p2, p6). GPT-2 and GPT-3 models scored 3.0% to 6.9% (p2).
domain: high-school competition mathematics: prealgebra, algebra, number theory, counting and probability, geometry, intermediate algebra, precalculus (p4)
size: 12,500 problems (7,500 train, 5,000 test) (p4); GPT-2 0.1B to 1.5B and GPT-3 13B and 175B, fine-tuned and few-shot (p5-7); BART in the appendix
source_of_items: competitions (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME and others; problems created by the MAA) (p4, p17)
instances: static (AMPS, a pretraining corpus only, includes about 5M script-generated problems, p6)
has_gold_traces: yes: a full step-by-step solution with a boxed final answer for every problem (p1, p4); used for training and as hints (p9), not to score model steps
evaluation: final answer: exact match of the boxed answer after normalisation rules for equivalent forms (p1, p5); a confidence AUROC analysis of error detection (p8)
human_validation: no check of items or of the scorer is reported; a rough human baseline on 20 sampled test problems, six university CS students of whom four are authors, scored 40% to 90% (p5, p15)
contamination_measures: none (public competition problems; contamination is not discussed)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): '... benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath ..., Putnam-Axiom ..., and GSM-Symbolic ... rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.' S-I3b (L105-111): 'specialized benchmarks (e.g., Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) or HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021)) assess abstract logic and algorithmic translation.'
engtrace_use.explanation: The gist (a hard, abstract mathematics benchmark) is right in both sentences, but the wording is loose. MATH presents itself as a test of 'problem-solving ability: the ability to analyze a problem, pick out good heuristics from a large set of possibilities, and chain them together' (p1) and contrasts itself with formal theorem proving (p3), so 'logical deduction' is not its own description; and it scores only the boxed final answer by exact match (p5), so 'rigorously test ... deduction' claims more than its scoring does. 'Reasoning stability' is not tested by MATH. For EngTrace the omission that matters runs the other way: MATH already pairs every problem with a full step-by-step solution (p1, p4) and shows that 'models can provide the right answer yet generate a misleading and wrong explanation' (p7), so the revised text cannot present pairing problems with reference solutions as new; what MATH lacks is any scoring of the model's steps.

suggested_wording: MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) supplies a full step-by-step solution for each of its 12,500 competition problems, yet scores only the boxed final answer by exact match, although its authors observe that models can reach the right answer with a wrong explanation.
facts_to_cite: 12,500 problems from mathematics competitions such as AMC 10, AMC 12 and AIME, split 7,500 train and 5,000 test, in seven subjects with difficulty levels 1 to 5 (p1, p4).
Every problem has a full step-by-step solution and a boxed final answer (p1, p4).
Scoring is exact match of the boxed answer after normalisation rules for equivalent forms (p1, p5).
At release, GPT-2 and GPT-3 models scored 3.0% to 6.9% (p2).
'Models can provide the right answer yet generate a misleading and wrong explanation' (Figure 3 caption, p7).
Having GPT-2 1.5B write a step-by-step solution before its answer lowered its accuracy, to 5.3% (p9).
The companion pretraining corpus AMPS contains about 5M problems generated by 100 hand-designed Mathematica scripts, 37 of which also generate step-by-step solutions (p4, p6).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: a reference step-by-step solution for every item (p1, p4); multi-step quantitative problems; difficulty levels (1 to 5, p4) comparable in role to EngTrace's Easy, Intermediate and Advanced tiers; script-generated problems with solutions, though only for pretraining (AMPS, p6). Lacks: generated evaluation instances (MATH itself is static); step-level evaluation (exact match on the boxed answer, p5); engineering domain; expert validation of items or of the scorer (none reported).
notes: Confidence is high on the facts; medium on imprecise rather than accurate. The May entry cites arXiv; the text is the NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks version (p1), which the revision should cite. MATH defines its problems against 'plug-and-chug calculations, a skill which ML models can already exhibit' (p1); since EngTrace's own Figure 1 example is a single design-equation substitution, the revision should contrast EngTrace with MATH on domain and on step verification, not on depth of problem solving. Hendrycks et al. 2021b (MATH) is a different paper from Hendrycks 2021a and 2020 (both MMLU).
